Sons Ltd.</copyright-statement><license><ali:license_ref xmlns:ali="http://www.niso.org/schemas/ali/1.0/" specific-use="textmining" content-type="ccbynclicense">https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/</ali:license_ref><license-p>This is an open access article under the terms of the <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/">http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/</ext-link> License, which permits use, distribution and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited and is not used for commercial purposes.</license-p></license></permissions><self-uri xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="pmc-pdf" xlink:href="DOM-27-2540.pdf"/><self-uri xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="pdf" xlink:href="file:DOM-27-2540.pdf"/><abstract><title>Abstract</title><sec id="dom16253-sec-0001"><title>Aim</title><p>To evaluate the efficacy and safety of semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo for weight management in a population of Chinese adults with overweight or obesity.</p></sec><sec id="dom16253-sec-0002"><title>Materials and Methods</title><p>In STEP 7 (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="pmc:clinical-trial" xlink:href="NCT04251156">NCT04251156</ext-link>), a double‐blind, phase 3a trial, adults from a predominantly East Asian population with overweight or obesity, with or without type 2 diabetes, were randomized 2:1 to once‐weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg or placebo for 44 weeks as an adjunct to a reduced‐calorie diet and increased physical activity. This prespecified analysis evaluated Chinese participants in STEP 7. The primary endpoints were percentage change in body weight from baseline to Week 44 and the proportion of participants who achieved ≥5% reduction in body weight from baseline.</p></sec><sec id="dom16253-sec-0003"><title>Results</title><p>Overall, 195 Chinese participants were randomized to semaglutide 2.4 mg and 105 to placebo. Estimated change in mean body weight from baseline to Week 44 was −11.8% with semaglutide 2.4 mg versus −3.5% with placebo (estimated treatment difference −8.3%; 95% confidence interval [CI] –10.2, −6.4; <italic toggle="no">p</italic> &lt; 0.0001). At Week 44, a greater proportion of participants treated with semaglutide 2.4 mg achieved ≥5% body weight loss versus placebo (85.4% vs. 26.8%): odds ratio 16.1; 95% CI 8.4, 30.9; <italic toggle="no">p</italic> &lt; 0.0001. Adverse events were reported by 92.3% of semaglutide‐treated participants and 82.9% of placebo‐treated participants, the most common of which were gastrointestinal disorders (126/195, 64.6% vs. 35/105, 33.3%).</p></sec><sec id="dom16253-sec-0004"><title>Conclusions</title><p>These data demonstrate beneficial effects of semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo, supporting its use in an adult Chinese population with overweight or obesity.</p></sec></abstract><kwd-group kwd-group-type="author-generated"><kwd id="dom16253-kwd-0001">antiobesity drug</kwd><kwd id="dom16253-kwd-0002">clinical trial</kwd><kwd id="dom16253-kwd-0003">GLP‐1 analogue</kwd><kwd id="dom16253-kwd-0004">phase III study</kwd><kwd id="dom16253-kwd-0005">semaglutide</kwd><kwd id="dom16253-kwd-0006">weight management</kwd></kwd-group><funding-group><award-group id="funding-0001"><funding-source>Novo Nordisk A/S</funding-source></award-group></funding-group><counts><fig-count count="2"/><table-count <mixed-citation publication-type="journal" id="dom16253-cit-9001">
<string-name name-style="western">

<given-names>W</given-names>
</string-name>, <string-name name-style="western">
<surname>Lu</surname>
<given-names>Y</given-names>
</string-name>, <string-name name-style="western">
<surname>Ye</surname>
<given-names>X</given-names>
</string-name>, et al. <article-title>Efficacy and safety of once‐weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg for weight management in participants from China: A prespecified analysis of the <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">STEP</styled-content> 7 randomized clinical trial</article-title>. <source>Diabetes Obes Metab</source>. <year>2025</year>;<volume>27</volume>(<issue>5</issue>):<fpage>2540</fpage>‐<lpage>2551</lpage>. doi:<pub-id pub-id-type="doi">10.1111/dom.16253</pub-id>
<pub-id pub-id-type="pmid">40069849</pub-id>
<pub-id pub-id-type="pmcid">PMC11964988</pub-id></mixed-citation>
</p></notes></front><body id="dom16253-body-0001"><sec id="dom16253-sec-0005"><label>1</label><title>INTRODUCTION</title><p>Obesity is a multifaceted health condition associated with multiple complications, including an increased risk of chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes (T2D), cardiovascular disease, certain cancers and musculoskeletal disorders. Obesity can negatively impact mental health, leading to depression, anxiety and diminished quality of life (QOL).<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0001" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>1</sup>
</xref>
</p><p>While the World Health Organization (WHO) defines obesity as a body mass index (BMI) of ≥30 kg/m<sup>2</sup>, if the Working Group on Obesity in China definitions are applied (BMI ≥24 kg/m<sup>2</sup> for overweight; BMI ≥28 kg/m<sup>2</sup> for obesity),<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0001" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>1</sup>
</xref>, <xref rid="dom16253-bib-0002" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>2</sup>
</xref> China had the highest global prevalence of overweight or obesity in 2021, with roughly 50% of adults affected. This is projected to increase to two‐thirds of the adult population by 2030.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0003" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>3</sup>
</xref> Pharmacological options for treating obesity in China are scarce; by 2023, only orlistat, beinaglutide and liraglutide were approved by the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) of China for weight management.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0004" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>4</sup>
</xref>, <xref rid="dom16253-bib-0005" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>5</sup>
</xref>, <xref rid="dom16253-bib-0006" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>6</sup>
</xref> As such, there is a strong unmet need for convenient medication for overweight and obesity in China.</p><p>The efficacy and safety of once‐weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg, a glucagon‐like peptide‐1 receptor agonist (GLP‐1RA), have been demonstrated for weight management in the STEP programme.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0007" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>7</sup>
</xref> Semaglutide 2.4 mg is approved for weight management in adults with obesity or overweight with ≥1 weight‐related comorbidity in the USA, Europe and other countries, including China (NMPA, June 2024).<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0008" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>8</sup>
</xref>, <xref rid="dom16253-bib-0009" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>9</sup>
</xref>, <xref rid="dom16253-bib-0010" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>10</sup>
</xref> In STEP 7 (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="pmc:clinical-trial" xlink:href="NCT04251156">NCT04251156</ext-link>), efficacy and safety were demonstrated in a predominantly East Asian population with overweight or obesity, with or without T2D.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0011" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>11</sup>
</xref>
</p><p>This prespecified analysis compared the efficacy and safety of semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo as an adjunct to a reduced‐calorie diet and increased physical activity in Chinese participants enrolled in STEP 7.</p></sec><sec sec-type="materials-and-methods" id="dom16253-sec-0006"><label>2</label><title>MATERIALS AND METHODS</title><sec id="dom16253-sec-0007"><label>2.1</label><title>Trial design</title><p>STEP 7 (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="pmc:clinical-trial" xlink:href="NCT04251156">NCT04251156</ext-link>) was a phase 3a, double‐blind, placebo‐controlled, multicentre randomized trial (Figure <xref rid="dom16253-supitem-0001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S2</xref>). Full details of the trial design have been previously described.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0011" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>11</sup>
</xref> This prespecified analysis of STEP 7 included a population of participants from mainland China (23 sites) and Hong Kong (one site). Briefly, eligible participants were aged ≥18 years with a history of ≥1 self‐reported unsuccessful dietary effort to lose weight, and a BMI of ≥30 kg/m<sup>2</sup> or ≥27 kg/m<sup>2</sup> with ≥1 of the following weight‐related comorbidities: hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea, cardiovascular disease, and T2D. Full eligibility criteria are in the supplementary materials (<bold>p2</bold>). This study was conducted in accordance with the International Council for Harmonization of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use guidelines.</p></sec><sec id="dom16253-sec-0008"><label>2.2</label><title>Procedures</title><p>Participants were randomized 2:1 to receive either semaglutide 2.4 mg or placebo, alongside a lifestyle intervention of approximately 500 kcal/day deficit in diet and 150 minutes/week of physical activity. Up to Week 16, participants followed a fixed‐dose escalation regimen for semaglutide with an initial dose of 0.25 mg, which was increased every 4 weeks to 0.5, 1.0, 1.7 and 2.4 mg/week. Participants then received a maintenance dose of semaglutide 2.4 mg until the end of treatment at 44 weeks. All participants provided written informed consent prior to trial‐related activities.</p></sec><sec id="dom16253-sec-0009"><label>2.3</label><title>Outcomes</title><p>The primary objective of this prespecified analysis was to compare the effect on body weight of semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo in participants with overweight or obesity with or without T2D. The secondary objectives were to compare the effect of semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo on cardiovascular risk factors, patient‐reported outcomes and glucose metabolism, and to assess safety and tolerability.</p><p>All endpoints were assessed from baseline to Week 44. The primary endpoints were the percentage change in body weight and the proportion of participants who achieved ≥5% reduction in body weight. Confirmatory secondary endpoints were the proportion of participants who achieved ≥10% and ≥15% reduction in body weight, and changes in waist circumference, systolic blood pressure, Short Form‐36 v2 Health Survey acute version (SF‐36v2) physical functioning score and Impact of Weight on Quality of Life‐Lite Clinical Trials Version (IWQOL‐Lite‐CT) physical function score. Supportive secondary endpoints included the proportion of participants who achieved ≥20% reduction in body weight, and change in body weight, BMI, glycated haemoglobin (HbA<sub>1c</sub>) (with and without T2D), fasting plasma glucose (FPG), fasting serum insulin, diastolic blood pressure, lipids and fatty liver index (FLI) score (&lt;30, ≥30, &lt;60, ≥60). FLI was calculated using BMI, waist circumference, triglycerides and gamma‐glutamyl transferase levels. Change in body weight was additionally assessed according to participant baseline characteristic subgroups, including age, sex, weight, BMI, diabetes status and renal function.</p><p>Safety endpoints reported until study end (Week 51) included the incidence of adverse events (AEs). Details of safety endpoints are included in the supplementary materials (<bold>p4</bold>).</p></sec><sec id="dom16253-sec-0010"><label>2.4</label><title>Statistical analysis</title><p>This was a prespecified analysis of the STEP 7 trial, not included in the statistical testing hierarchy. As such, the superiority of semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo cannot be ascertained in this population; however, statistical significance between groups could be determined. The following datasets were defined in the STEP 7 protocol and used in this prespecified analysis: the full analysis set, which included all randomized participants according to the intention‐to‐treat protocol, and the safety analysis set, which included all randomized participants exposed to at least one dose of the assigned randomized treatment.</p><p>Two observation periods were defined: the in‐trial period was the uninterrupted time from randomization to the last interaction with the trial site or investigators, and the on‐treatment period was the time from first administration of the trial product to 2 weeks after the last dose for efficacy analyses, or 7 weeks after the last dose for safety analyses. Any off‐treatment time intervals (defined as ≥2 consecutive missed doses for efficacy analyses or ≥7 consecutive missed doses for safety analyses) were excluded from the on‐treatment period.</p><p>Two estimands (treatment policy estimand and trial product estimand; supplementary materials [<bold>p5</bold>]) were used to assess treatment efficacy and accounted differently for intercurrent events and missing data, as described previously.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0011" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>11</sup>
</xref>, <xref rid="dom16253-bib-0012" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>12</sup>
</xref>
</p><p>The primary endpoints were analysed using a covariance and logistic regression model, as described previously.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0011" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>11</sup>
</xref> Primary and confirmatory endpoints were part of statistical testing hierarchy, but supportive secondary endpoints were not. Results from statistical analyses are shown with two‐sided 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and corresponding <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> values. Additional details are available in the supplementary materials (<bold>p5</bold>).</p></sec></sec><sec sec-type="results" id="dom16253-sec-0011"><label>3</label><title>RESULTS</title><sec id="dom16253-sec-0012"><label>3.1</label><title>Baseline characteristics</title><p>From 8 December 2020 to 23 August 2022, 351 participants from China were screened, of whom 300 were randomized 2:1 to receive either semaglutide 2.4 mg (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 195) or placebo (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 105) (Figure <xref rid="dom16253-supitem-0001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S3</xref>). This included 270 participants (90.0%) from mainland China and 30 (10.0%) from Hong Kong. In total, 292 participants (97.3%) were trial completers (semaglutide 2.4 mg, 97.4%; placebo, 97.1%). Of participants in the semaglutide group, 95.3% and 91.2% received a dose of 2.4 mg at Weeks 20 and 44, respectively (Figure <xref rid="dom16253-supitem-0001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1</xref>).</p><p>Overall, mean (standard deviation [SD]) body weight was 96.4 kg (17.4), mean waist circumference was 107.5 cm (11.1) and mean BMI was 33.8 kg/m<sup>2</sup> (4.6). Most participants (80.7%) had obesity, as defined by WHO criteria. A similar proportion of participants had T2D at screening between the treatment groups (semaglutide 2.4 mg 26.7% vs. placebo 24.8%). In participants with T2D, mean (SD) duration of diabetes was 5.7 years (4.9) and mean HbA<sub>1c</sub> was 8.0% (0.7). The proportion of participants with prediabetes was also similar between groups (29.2% vs. 34.3%). Dyslipidaemia and metabolic dysfunction‐associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) were the most reported comorbidities, affecting 63.7% and 58.3% of participants, respectively. In total, 260 (86.7%) participants had an FLI score ≥60 at baseline, and among these, 159 participants had an MASLD diagnosis (Table <xref rid="dom16253-supitem-0001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1</xref>). Baseline characteristics were balanced across treatment groups (Table <xref rid="dom16253-tbl-0001" ref-type="table">1</xref>).</p><table-wrap position="float" id="dom16253-tbl-0001" content-type="TABLE" orientation="portrait"><label>TABLE 1</label><caption><p>Baseline characteristics.</p></caption><table frame="hsides" rules="groups"><col align="left" span="1"/><col align="left" align="left" style="padding-left:10%" valign="top" rowspan="1" colspan="1">Thiazolidinediones</td><td align="left" valign="top" rowspan="1" colspan="1">4 (2.1)</td><td align="left" valign="top" rowspan="1" colspan="1">2 (1.9)</td><td align="left" valign="top" rowspan="1" colspan="1">6 (2.0)</td></tr><tr><td align="left" style="padding-left:10%" valign="top" rowspan="1" align="left" valign="top" rowspan="1" colspan="1">1 (0.3)</td></tr></tbody></table><table-wrap-foot id="dom16253-ntgp-0002"><fn id="dom16253-note-0001"><p>
<italic toggle="yes">Note</italic>: Data are <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> (%) or mean ± SD and include all participants in the full analysis set, unless otherwise stated.</p></fn><fn id="dom16253-note-0002"><p>Abbreviations: CV, coefficient of variation; eGFR, estimated glomerular filtration rate; FPG, fasting plasma glucose; HbA<sub>1c</sub>, glycated haemoglobin; HDL, high‐density lipoprotein; IWQOL‐Lite‐CT, Impact of Weight on Quality of Life‐Lite Clinical Trials Version; LDL, low‐density lipoprotein; MASLD, metabolic dysfunction‐associated steatotic liver disease; SD, standard deviation; SF‐36v2, Short Form‐36 v2 Health Survey acute version; SGLT2, sodium–glucose cotransporter‐2; T2D, type 2 diabetes; VLDL, very‐low‐density lipoprotein.</p></fn><fn id="dom16253-note-0003"><label>
<sup>a</sup>
</label><p>Presence of specific weight‐related comorbidities were collected systematically at screening by the investigator as part of the medical history and included: dyslipidaemia, MASLD, hypertension, elevated HbA<sub>1c</sub>, T2D, hyperuricaemia/gout, menstrual disorder, polycystic ovarian syndrome, obstructive sleep apnoea, impaired fasting glucose, kidney disease and symptomatic osteoarthritis of the knee.</p></fn></table-wrap-foot></table-wrap></sec><sec id="dom16253-sec-0013"><label>3.2</label><title>Primary endpoints</title><p>The mean body weight change at Week 44 was −11.8% with semaglutide 2.4 mg versus −3.5% with placebo (estimated treatment difference [ETD] –8.3 percentage points; 95% CI –10.2, −6.4; <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> &lt; 0.0001), for the treatment policy estimand (Figure <xref rid="dom16253-fig-0001" ref-type="fig">1A</xref>); results were consistent for the trial product estimand (Figure <xref rid="dom16253-supitem-0001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S4</xref>; Table <xref rid="dom16253-supitem-0001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S2</xref>). During the in‐trial observation period, a greater proportion of participants receiving semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo had a body weight loss of ≥5% (85.4% vs. 26.8%); the odds of achieving this threshold also favoured semaglutide 2.4 mg (odds ratio [OR] 16.1; 95% CI 8.4, 30.9; <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> &lt; 0.0001) for the treatment policy estimand (Figure <xref rid="dom16253-fig-0001" ref-type="fig">1B</xref>). Similar results were seen for the on‐treatment observation period and trial product estimand (Figure <xref rid="dom16253-supitem-0001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S5</xref>; Table <xref rid="dom16253-supitem-0001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S2</xref>). Additionally, the effect of semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo on body weight change from baseline was consistent across subgroups (Table <xref rid="dom16253-supitem-0001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S3</xref>).</p><fig position="float" fig-type="FIGURE" id="dom16253-fig-0001" orientation="portrait"><label>FIGURE 1</label><caption><p>(A) Mean change in body weight from baseline to Week 44, and (B) proportion of participants achieving body weight loss ≥5%, ≥10%, ≥15% and ≥20% at Week 44. Observed data are from the in‐trial observation period. Error bars are +/− standard error of the mean. Data are from the full analysis set. Numbers shown under panel A are participants contributing to the mean. The ETD in panel A and ORs in panel B are for the treatment policy estimand. <sup>†</sup>Estimated means. CI, confidence interval; ETD, estimated treatment difference; OR, odds ratio.</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" position="anchor" id="jats-graphic-1" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="DOM-27-2540-g001.jpg"/></fig></sec><sec id="dom16253-sec-0014"><label>3.3</label><title>Confirmatory secondary endpoints</title><p>The observed proportion of participants achieving a ≥10% or ≥15% change in body weight at Week 44 was greater with semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo, as odds favoured semaglutide 2.4 mg (Table <xref rid="dom16253-tbl-0002" ref-type="table">2</xref>; Figure <xref rid="dom16253-fig-0001" ref-type="fig">1B</xref>). Additionally, improvements were greater in the semaglutide 2.4 mg group compared with the placebo group for waist circumference (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> &lt; 0.0001), systolic blood pressure (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.0466) and SF‐36v2 physical functioning score (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.0024) (Table <xref rid="dom16253-tbl-0002" ref-type="table">2</xref>; Figure <xref rid="dom16253-fig-0002" ref-type="fig">2</xref>). The estimated mean change in the IWQOL‐Lite‐CT physical function score from baseline to Week 44 was not statistically significant between treatment groups (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.1623; Table <xref rid="dom16253-tbl-0002" ref-type="table">2</xref> and Figure <xref rid="dom16253-fig-0002" ref-type="fig">2</xref>).</p><table-wrap position="float" id="dom16253-tbl-0002" content-type="TABLE" orientation="portrait"><label>TABLE 2</label><caption><p>Primary, confirmatory secondary and selected supportive secondary trial endpoints (treatment policy estimand<xref rid="dom16253-note-0006" ref-type="table-fn">

<italic toggle="yes">Note</italic>: All participants in the full analysis set are included in the treatment comparisons.</p></fn><fn id="dom16253-note-0005"><p>Abbreviations: BMI, body mass index; CI, confidence interval; ETD, estimated treatment difference; FLI, fatty liver index; FPG, fasting plasma glucose; HbA<sub>1c</sub>, glycated haemoglobin; HDL, high‐density lipoprotein; IWQOL‐Lite‐CT, Impact of Weight on Quality of Life‐Lite Clinical Trials Version; LDL, low‐density lipoprotein; MASLD, metabolic dysfunction‐associated steatotic liver disease; OR, odds ratio; SF‐36v2, Short Form‐36 v2 Health Survey acute version; T2D, type 2 diabetes; VLDL, very‐low‐density lipoprotein.</p></fn><fn id="dom16253-note-0006"><label>
<sup>a</sup>
</label><p>The treatment policy estimand assesses treatment effect regardless of treatment discontinuation or rescue intervention (weight‐management drugs or bariatric surgery).</p></fn><fn id="dom16253-note-0007"><label>
<sup>b</sup>
</label><p>All confirmatory secondary endpoints are included in the testing hierarchy and are listed in the order in which they were analysed.</p></fn><fn id="dom16253-note-0008"><label>
<sup>c</sup>
</label><p>For all non‐confirmatory endpoints, <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> values were not controlled for multiplicity.</p></fn><fn id="dom16253-note-0009"><label>
<sup>d</sup>
</label><p>Week 44 responses were analysed using an analysis of covariance model with randomized treatment and T2D status as factors and baseline fasting serum insulin/baseline lipid value as covariates. The ratio to baseline and the corresponding baseline value were log‐transformed prior to analysis. Missing observations were multiple (x1000) imputed from retrieved participants of the same randomized treatment group. The approximate relative changes/differences were derived from estimated ratios by subtracting 1 and multiplying by 100.</p></fn><fn id="dom16253-note-0010"><label>
<sup>e</sup>
</label><p>FLI was based on an algorithm including BMI, waist circumference, triglycerides and gamma‐glutamyl‐transferase, and was used to select and predict participants at greater risk of MASLD.</p></fn><fn id="dom16253-note-0011"><label>
<sup>f</sup>
</label><p>Overall change in oral anti‐diabetes drug intensity from Week 0 to Week 24.</p></fn></table-wrap-foot></table-wrap><fig position="float" fig-type="FIGURE" id="dom16253-fig-0002" orientation="portrait"><label>FIGURE 2</label><caption><p>Mean change in (A) waist circumference, (B) systolic blood pressure, (C) SF‐36v2 physical functioning scores and (D) IWQOL‐Lite‐CT physical function scores from baseline to Week 44. Observed data are from the in‐trial observation period. Error bars are +/− standard error of the mean. Numbers shown in the lower panel are participants contributing to the mean. IWQOL‐Lite‐CT, Impact of Weight on Quality of Life‐Lite Clinical Trials Version; SF‐36v2, Short Form‐36 v2 Health Survey acute version.</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" position="anchor" id="jats-graphic-3" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="DOM-27-2540-g002.jpg"/></fig></sec><sec id="dom16253-sec-0015"><label>3.4</label><title>Selected supportive secondary endpoints</title><p>Overall, the odds of participants achieving ≥20% reduction in body weight from baseline to Week 44 favoured semaglutide 2.4 mg (OR 5.6; 95% CI 1.3, 23.7; <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.0194) for the treatment policy estimand (Figure <xref rid="dom16253-fig-0001" ref-type="fig">1B</xref>). Mean BMI changes from baseline at Week 44 were −4.0 kg/m<sup>2</sup> and −1.2 kg/m<sup>2</sup> with semaglutide 2.4 mg and placebo, respectively (ETD –2.8 kg/m<sup>2</sup>; 95% CI –3.5, −2.0; <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> &lt; 0.0001; Table <xref rid="dom16253-tbl-0002" ref-type="table">2</xref>).</p><p>A greater reduction from baseline to Week 44 in total cholesterol, very‐low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol and triglycerides was observed for participants in the semaglutide 2.4 mg group compared with the placebo group (Table <xref rid="dom16253-tbl-0002" ref-type="table">2</xref>). No changes in levels of high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol, low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol or free fatty acids were observed in either treatment group.</p><p>Of the participants with an FLI ≥60 at baseline, scores improved to between ≥30 and &lt;60 in 29.1% and 9.6% of participants in the semaglutide 2.4 mg and placebo groups (OR 3.8; 95% CI 1.7, 8.6; <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.0010), respectively. Improvements to &lt;30 were recorded for 19.0% of participants treated with semaglutide 2.4 mg and 4.8% of participants treated with placebo (OR 4.6; 95% CI 1.6, 3.6; <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.0054).</p><p>The estimated mean changes in HbA<sub>1c</sub> from baseline to Week 44 were −0.8% and −0.1% with semaglutide 2.4 mg and placebo, respectively (ETD −0.7%; 95% CI −0.8, −0.5; <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> &lt; 0.0001), and estimated change in FPG from baseline to Week 44 was −1.1 mmol/L (−18.9 mg/dL) with semaglutide 2.4 mg and −0.1 mmol/L (−1.4 mg/dL) with placebo (ETD –1.0 mmol/L; 95% CI –1.2, −0.7; <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> &lt; 0.0001) (Table <xref rid="dom16253-tbl-0002" ref-type="table">2</xref>).</p><p>Of the participants with prediabetes at baseline, 79.6% of the semaglutide 2.4 mg group achieved normoglycaemia by Week 44, compared with 25.0% of the placebo group (OR 11.7; 95% CI 4.2, 33.1; <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> &lt; 0.0001), and 20.4% of participants in the semaglutide 2.4 mg group continued to have prediabetes versus 68.8% in the placebo group (OR 0.1; 95% CI 0.0, 0.3; <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> &lt; 0.0001). Furthermore, no participants receiving semaglutide 2.4 mg progressed to having T2D, with 6.3% (two participants) in the placebo group progressing to having T2D.</p><p>For the participants with T2D at screening, the observed mean changes in HbA<sub>1c</sub> from baseline to Week 44 were −2.0% for semaglutide 2.4 mg and −0.6% for placebo. Additionally, the odds of achieving HbA<sub>1c</sub> &lt;7.0% (53 mmol/mol) or ≤6.5% (48 mmol/mol) were significantly greater with semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo (Table <xref rid="dom16253-tbl-0002" ref-type="table">2</xref>). Most participants (semaglutide 2.4 mg, 61.5%; placebo, 57.7%) did not change their oral anti‐diabetes drugs (OADs) between baseline and Week 44. A greater proportion of participants who received semaglutide 2.4 mg decreased their OAD than those who received placebo (21.6% vs. 4.0%) (Table <xref rid="dom16253-tbl-0002" ref-type="table">2</xref>). Furthermore, no participants in the semaglutide 2.4 mg group increased their OAD medication compared with 20.0% in the placebo group.</p></sec><sec id="dom16253-sec-0016"><label>3.5</label><title>Adverse events</title><p>AEs were reported by 180/195 (92.3%) participants in the semaglutide 2.4 mg group and 87/105 (82.9%) participants in the placebo group (Table <xref rid="dom16253-tbl-0003" ref-type="table">3</xref>). The most frequently reported AEs were gastrointestinal (GI) disorders (semaglutide 2.4 mg, 64.6%; placebo, 33.3%). The most frequent GI disorders in the semaglutide 2.4 mg and placebo groups were diarrhoea (28.2% vs. 6.7%) and nausea (20.5% vs. 4.8%) (Table <xref rid="dom16253-tbl-0003" ref-type="table">3</xref>). Most events were mild or moderate in severity, with the outcome reported as recovered or resolved (Table <xref rid="dom16253-supitem-0001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S4</xref>). The incidence of AEs was generally balanced between participants with and without T2D, although serious AEs (SAEs) were less frequently reported by those with versus without T2D (Table <xref rid="dom16253-supitem-0001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S5</xref>). Retinal disorder AEs for participants with T2D were reported in 11.5% of the participants in the semaglutide 2.4 mg group, with no events reported in the placebo group. The most frequently reported retinal disorder was diabetic retinopathy, with greater rates at baseline in the semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo groups (19.2% vs. 11.5%). SAEs were reported by 12 (6.2%) and 7 (6.7%) participants in the semaglutide 2.4 mg and placebo groups, respectively.</p><table-wrap position="float" id="dom16253-tbl-0003" content-type="TABLE" <sup>a</sup>
</xref>
</td><td align="left" valign="top" rowspan="1" colspan="1">1 (0.5)</td><td align="left" valign="top" rowspan="1" colspan="1">1</td><td align="left" valign="top" rowspan="1" colspan="1">0.5</td><td align="left" valign="top" rowspan="1" colspan="1">1 (1.0)</td><td align="left" valign="top" rowspan="1" colspan="1">1</td><td align="left" valign="top" rowspan="1" colspan="1">1.0</td></tr></tbody></table><table-wrap-foot id="dom16253-ntgp-0004"><fn id="dom16253-note-0012"><p>
<italic toggle="yes">Note</italic>: Data are <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> (%) of the safety analysis population (all randomly allocated participants exposed to at least one dose of randomized intervention) experiencing at least one event. Data are for on‐treatment AEs, occurring during treatment with any dose of trial intervention given within the previous 49 days (after excluding any temporary interruptions in taking trial intervention), unless otherwise stated.</p></fn><fn id="dom16253-note-0013"><p>Abbreviations: AE, adverse event; GI, gastrointestinal; GLP‐1RA, glucagon‐like peptide‐1 receptor agonists; MedDRA, Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities; T2D, type 2 diabetes.</p></fn><fn id="dom16253-note-0014"><label>
<sup>a</sup>
</label><p>In‐trial observation period.</p></fn><fn id="dom16253-note-0015"><label>
<sup>b</sup>
</label><p>On the basis of therapeutic experience with GLP‐1RAs and regulatory feedback and requirements, a number of safety focus areas were prespecified as being of special interest in the safety evaluation. Identified through searches of MedDRA, these preferred terms were judged to be relevant for each of the safety focus areas.</p></fn><fn id="dom16253-note-0016"><label>
<sup>c</sup>
</label><p>For retinal disorders, the percentage is based on the number of participants with T2D at screening.</p></fn><fn id="dom16253-note-0017"><label>
<sup>d</sup>
</label><p>Acute renal failure was the MedDRA search term, but the actual reported term from the site was ‘renal insufficiency’.</p></fn></table-wrap-foot></table-wrap><p>AEs leading to permanent trial product discontinuation were experienced by seven (3.6%) and two (1.9%) participants in the semaglutide 2.4 mg and placebo groups, respectively. Discontinuations in the semaglutide 2.4 mg group were due to GI disorders (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3) and one event each of chest discomfort, fatigue, cholecystitis, cholelithiasis, papillary thyroid cancer, anxiety and loss of libido. The two cases in the placebo group were due to bladder cancer and a pregnancy‐related condition (Table <xref rid="dom16253-supitem-0001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S6</xref>). The two malignancy events were assessed as unlikely to be related to the trial product, and their outcomes were reported as recovered (papillary thyroid cancer) and recovering (bladder cancer). No deaths were reported during the trial. Data on amylase and lipase levels are shown in the Table <xref rid="dom16253-supitem-0001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S7</xref>.</p><sec id="dom16253-sec-0017"><label>3.5.1</label><title>Hypoglycaemia</title><p>In participants without T2D, there was no difference in the proportion of hypoglycaemic events between treatment groups (semaglutide 2.4 mg, 4.2%; placebo, 3.8%). In participants with T2D at baseline (semaglutide 2.4 mg, <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 52; placebo, <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 26), one (1.9%) hypoglycaemic episode was classified as a severe or blood glucose‐confirmed symptomatic episode (&lt;3.1 mmol/L [56 mg/dL]) in the semaglutide 2.4 mg group.</p></sec></sec></sec><sec sec-type="discussion" id="dom16253-sec-0018"><label>4</label><title>DISCUSSION</title><p>This prespecified analysis of the STEP 7 trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of semaglutide 2.4 mg as an adjunct to lifestyle intervention in adults with overweight or obesity from China.</p><p>The characteristics of participants in this analysis were similar to the overall STEP 7 population<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0011" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>11</sup>
</xref>; however, compared with the STEP 1–4 trials, the STEP 7 Chinese population had more male participants (19.0–48.8% vs. 58.7%), lower BMI (35.9–38.4 kg/m<sup>2</sup> vs. 33.8 kg/m<sup>2</sup>), smaller waist circumference (113.0–115.3 cm vs. 107.5 cm) and greater prevalence of comorbidities, in particular MASLD (5.7–21.6% vs. 58.3%).<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0013" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>13</sup>
</xref>, <xref rid="dom16253-bib-0014" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>14</sup>
</xref>, <xref rid="dom16253-bib-0015" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>15</sup>
</xref> Additionally, a global analysis of the incidence of MASLD found the presence of this disease in China to be consistent with the global incidence rate (29.2–32.5% vs. 32%).<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0016" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>16</sup>
</xref> Although this rate is not currently as high as some countries, including Turkey (48.4%) and the USA (47.8%), it is predicted that China will have the greatest overall increase in MASLD presence by 2030.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0016" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>16</sup>
</xref> This prevalence of fatty liver disease complements data observed in a real‐world study of 15.8 million adults in China, in which 81.8% of participants with obesity were found to have this disease.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0017" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>17</sup>
</xref> This highlights the need for effective management of overweight and obesity in China.</p><p>In this analysis, an estimated mean reduction from baseline to Week 44 in body weight of 11.8% was observed with semaglutide 2.4 mg. This was consistent with the body weight reduction of 12.1% reported in the overall STEP 7 population,<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0011" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>11</sup>
</xref> and of approximately 10–16% up to Week 68 reported in previous STEP trials.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0013" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>13</sup>
</xref>, <xref rid="dom16253-bib-0014" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>14</sup>
</xref>, <xref rid="dom16253-bib-0015" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>15</sup>
</xref>, <xref rid="dom16253-bib-0018" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>18</sup>
</xref> The beneficial effect of semaglutide 2.4 mg compared with placebo was generally seen across all subgroups (Table <xref rid="dom16253-supitem-0001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S3</xref>), which is consistent with STEP 1 and 2 responder analysis.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0013" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>13</sup>
</xref>, <xref rid="dom16253-bib-0014" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>14</sup>
</xref>
</p><p>A body weight reduction of 5%–10% is recommended by Chinese guidelines for the management of obesity in adults.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0019" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>19</sup>
</xref> In total, 85.4% of participants in the semaglutide 2.4 mg group in this analysis achieved a ≥5% body weight reduction from baseline. This is in line with the full population in the STEP 7 trial (85.3%),<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0011" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>11</sup>
</xref> and is broadly consistent with other STEP trials, including the STEP 6 trial in participants from East Asia.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0018" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>18</sup>
</xref> In comparison with a similar population of Chinese adults, 58.2% of participants treated with the alternative GLP‐1RA beinaglutide achieved a ≥5% reduction in body weight from baseline over a 16‐week study.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0020" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>20</sup>
</xref> Improvements in other cardiovascular risk factors were also observed with semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo in this analysis, including systolic blood pressure, waist circumference, total cholesterol, very‐low density cholesterol and triglycerides.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0020" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>20</sup>
</xref>
</p><p>Obesity can significantly affect various aspects of QOL, with several studies highlighting the correlation between increased obesity and decreased QOL.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0001" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>1</sup>
</xref>, <xref rid="dom16253-bib-0021" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>21</sup>
</xref>, <xref rid="dom16253-bib-0022" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>22</sup>
</xref> In this analysis, the SF‐36v2 physical functioning score showed a significantly greater improvement with semaglutide 2.4 mg compared with placebo. These data align with results seen in the overall STEP 7 population,<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0011" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>11</sup>
</xref> as well as in an analysis of the STEP 1–4 trials.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0023" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>23</sup>
</xref> No statistically significant difference was observed in the change in baseline IWQOL‐Lite‐CT physical function score to Week 44 between semaglutide 2.4 mg and placebo. This is consistent with the results reported in STEP 7<sup>11</sup> and may reflect the fact that mean baseline IWQOL‐Lite‐CT physical function scores were greater than in STEP 1 and 2.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0013" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>13</sup>
</xref>, <xref rid="dom16253-bib-0014" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>14</sup>
</xref> Therefore, participants may have had less scope for improvement.</p><p>A greater proportion of participants treated with semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo demonstrated improvements in FLI scores from baseline to Week 44, consistent with previous studies showing improvements in outcomes related to MASLD with semaglutide.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0024" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>24</sup>
</xref> Irrespective of T2D status at baseline, treatment with semaglutide 2.4 mg improved HbA<sub>1c</sub>, FPG and fasting serum insulin levels compared with placebo from baseline to Week 44. Of the participants who had prediabetes at baseline, a greater proportion treated with semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo achieved normoglycaemia by Week 44. No participants receiving semaglutide 2.4 mg progressed to T2D. This generally aligns with results observed in many STEP trials, including the STEP 10 trial, which was conducted specifically in participants with prediabetes.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0011" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>11</sup>
</xref>, <xref rid="dom16253-bib-0013" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>13</sup>
</xref>, <xref rid="dom16253-bib-0018" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>18</sup>
</xref>, <xref rid="dom16253-bib-0025" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>25</sup>
</xref>, <xref rid="dom16253-bib-0026" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>26</sup>
</xref>, <xref rid="dom16253-bib-0027" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>27</sup>
</xref> In our analysis, participants with T2D receiving semaglutide 2.4 mg had an improvement in HbA<sub>1c</sub> of −2.0% over 44 weeks, while in STEP 2, which comprised of a population with T2D, HbA<sub>1c</sub> improved by −1.6% over 68 weeks with semaglutide 2.4 mg.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0014" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>14</sup>
</xref> Additionally, semaglutide 2.4 mg treatment increased the proportion of participants with T2D who achieved HbA<sub>1c</sub> of &lt;7% or ≤6.5% versus placebo; the odds of achieving HbA<sub>1c</sub> &lt;7% or ≤6.5% with semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo was greater in this analysis (OR 21.2 and 20.6, respectively) than in the 68‐week STEP 2 trial (OR 10.9 and 9.8, respectively).<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0014" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>14</sup>
</xref>
</p><p>The majority of participants in the semaglutide group had successfully escalated to the 2.4 mg dose, indicating that semaglutide was well‐tolerated in this population. The AE profile in this population of Chinese participants was similar to that observed previously in the STEP trials (including STEP 7), and for the GLP‐1RA class in general.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0028" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>28</sup>
</xref> No new safety concerns were identified. There was a greater incidence of AEs with semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo, primarily attributed to GI AEs, although these were mostly non‐serious and reported as resolved or recovered. The proportion and rate of SAEs and AEs leading to discontinuation of the trial product were comparable between the treatment groups. As seen in the overall STEP 7 population,<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0011" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>11</sup>
</xref> there was an increase in rates of cardiovascular AEs for semaglutide 2.4 mg compared with placebo, of which palpitations were the most common. However, these events were primarily mild or moderate and considered to be unlikely to be related to the study drug. In participants with T2D, incidence of retinal disorders were higher with semaglutide 2.4 mg than placebo; the long‐term effects of treatment on diabetic retinopathy are being separately assessed.<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0029" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>29</sup>
</xref>
</p><p>Limitations of the study included a treatment duration of 44 weeks, restricting long‐term assessment in this population, and use of the WHO definitions rather than the Chinese‐specific BMI cut‐off values for overweight (≥24 kg/m<sup>2</sup>) and obesity (≥28 kg/m<sup>2</sup>).<xref rid="dom16253-bib-0002" ref-type="bibr">
<sup>2</sup>
</xref> Furthermore, there were insufficient numbers of participants on a dose of semaglutide &lt;2.4 mg, so it was not possible to evaluate the efficacy of the lower dose of semaglutide (1.7 mg) in a Chinese population. Semaglutide 2.4 mg demonstrated statistically significant weight loss and cardiovascular risk factor benefits compared with placebo; however, this predefined analysis was not intended to establish superiority between groups.</p><p>However, the STEP 7 trial was well‐conducted, as reflected by the high proportion of trial completers, including those who were on the trial product during the full 44‐week treatment period. Rates of missing data were low in both treatment groups, lending credibility to the observed results.</p></sec><sec sec-type="conclusions" id="dom16253-sec-0019"><label>5</label><title>CONCLUSIONS</title><p>In a population of Chinese adults with overweight or obesity, with or without T2D, treatment with once‐weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg as an adjunct to a reduced‐calorie diet and increased physical activity provided beneficial effects compared with placebo. These benefits included improvements in body weight loss, waist circumference, systolic blood pressure, lipids, glucose metabolism, MASLD, FLI scores, and SF‐36v2 physical functioning score. Furthermore, the AE profile was consistent with the GLP‐1RA class. These findings support a favourable benefit–risk profile of semaglutide 2.4 mg for weight management in this population.</p></sec><sec id="dom16253-sec-0020"><title>AUTHOR CONTRIBUTIONS</title><p>Dongmei Lui and Zewei Shen contributed to analysis of data. Zu Ning contributed to study design, conduct/data collection and analysis of data. Weijun Gu, Yibing Lu, Xinhua Ye, Guoyue Yuan and Yiming Mu contributed to the conduct/data collection, writing review and approval of the manuscript. The manuscript was written by a medical writer under the direction of the authors, who all provided critical revision and approved the final version for publication.</p></sec><sec sec-type="COI-statement" id="dom16253-sec-0022"><title>CONFLICT OF INTEREST STATEMENT</title><p>Dongmei Lui, Ning Zu and Zewei Shen are employees of Novo Nordisk and own Novo Nordisk stock. Yiming Mu has received speaker honorarium or consultancy fees in advisory boards from Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk and Sanofi. Weijun Gu, Yibing Lu, Xinhua Ye and Guoyue Yuan have no conflicts of interest to disclose.</p></sec><sec id="dom16253-sec-0023"><sec disp-level="2" id="dom16253-sec-0025"><title>PEER REVIEW</title><p>The peer review history for this article is available at <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://www.webofscience.com/api/gateway/wos/peer-review/10.1111/dom.16253" ext-link-type="uri">https://www.webofscience.com/api/gateway/wos/peer‐review/10.1111/dom.16253</ext-link>.</p></sec></sec><sec sec-type="supplementary-material"><title>Supporting information</title><supplementary-material id="dom16253-supitem-0001" position="float" content-type="local-data" orientation="portrait"><caption><p>

<string-name name-style="western">
<surname>Mu</surname>
